questions.title: Cause not producing secondary hypertension
questions.question: The followings may lead to secondary hypertension except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a cause of secondary hypertension). Polycystic kidney disease is a renal cause of secondary hypertension, and renal disease is the commonest cause of the secondary form overall.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a cause of secondary hypertension). Cushing syndrome raises blood pressure through excess cortisol (mineralocorticoid-like sodium and water retention), a recognised endocrine cause of secondary hypertension.
explanations.C: Correct. Secondary hypertension is high blood pressure with an identifiable underlying cause, and its named causes are renal (e.g. polycystic kidney, chronic glomerulonephritis, renal artery stenosis), endocrine (Cushing syndrome, phaeochromocytoma, hyperaldosteronism, hyperthyroidism), cardiovascular (coarctation of the aorta) and toxaemia of pregnancy. HYPOthyroidism is not on this list — it is if anything associated with a tendency to a low metabolic/cardiac-output state, so it is the exception here. This is exactly the endocrine-cause distinction the question tests: hyperthyroidism can raise pressure, hypothyroidism does not cause secondary hypertension.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS a cause of secondary hypertension). Toxaemia of pregnancy (pre-eclampsia) is a named pregnancy-related cause of secondary hypertension.

questions.learning_objective: List the causes of secondary hypertension (renal, endocrine, cardiovascular, pregnancy) and recognise hypothyroidism as not among them.

questions.title: Commonest cause of secondary hypertension
questions.question: The commonest cause of secondary hypertension is:

explanations.A: Correct. Among the secondary (identifiable-cause) hypertensions, renal disease is by far the commonest category, including chronic glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney disease, diabetic nephropathy and renal artery stenosis. The kidney's central role in long-term blood-pressure control — through sodium and water handling and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system — is why renal parenchymal and renovascular disease dominate the secondary causes. This is distinct from the far more common ESSENTIAL (primary) hypertension, which by definition has no single identifiable cause.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Liver disease is not a recognised cause of secondary hypertension in this classification.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cerebral disease can be a CONSEQUENCE of hypertension (e.g. cerebral haemorrhage) but is not a common cause of secondary hypertension.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Blood diseases are not among the named causes of secondary hypertension.

questions.learning_objective: State that renal disease is the commonest cause of secondary hypertension.

questions.title: Renal cause not producing hypertension
questions.question: Renal HTN is caused by all of the followings except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a cause of renal hypertension). Diabetic nephropathy damages the renal parenchyma and is a recognised renal (parenchymal) cause of hypertension.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a cause of renal hypertension). Chronic glomerulonephritis is a classic renal parenchymal cause of secondary hypertension.
explanations.C: Correct. Hypernephroma (renal cell carcinoma) is a malignant tumour of the renal tubular epithelium; it is not one of the causes of renal hypertension. Renal hypertension arises either from diffuse parenchymal disease (glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, polycystic kidney) or from renovascular disease reducing renal perfusion (renal artery atherosclerosis or stenosis, activating the renin–angiotensin system). A localised tubular-cell carcinoma does not fit either mechanism, which is why it is the exception here.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS a cause of renal hypertension). Atherosclerosis of the renal artery is a renovascular cause: reduced renal perfusion activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and raises blood pressure.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish renal parenchymal and renovascular causes of hypertension from renal cell carcinoma (hypernephroma), which does not cause renal hypertension.

questions.title: Cause of hyaline arteriolar change
questions.question: Hyaline change in arteriolar wall is due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Malignant (accelerated) hypertension produces FIBRINOID necrosis of arteriolar walls and hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis, not the bland hyaline change of the benign form.
explanations.B: Correct. Benign (long-standing, moderate) hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis — a homogeneous, glassy pink (hyaline) thickening of the arteriolar wall from leakage of plasma proteins across the injured endothelium and increased smooth-muscle matrix production. This narrows the lumen and is the hallmark small-vessel lesion of benign hypertension (and of diabetes). It contrasts with the fibrinoid necrosis and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis seen in malignant hypertension.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotising vasculitis of medium-sized arteries with fibrinoid necrosis, not hyaline arteriolar thickening.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Atherosclerosis affects large and medium ELASTIC and muscular arteries (intimal atheromatous plaques), not the hyaline change of small arterioles.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute hyaline arteriolosclerosis to benign hypertension, distinguishing it from the fibrinoid necrosis of the malignant form.

questions.title: Arterial change not seen in benign hypertension
questions.question: In benign hypertension, the arterial wall shows the following pathological changes except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a benign-hypertension change). Fibrosis (increased fibrous tissue in the wall) is part of the slow, reactive wall thickening of benign hypertension.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a benign-hypertension change). Hyalinosis (hyaline arteriolosclerosis) is the hallmark small-vessel lesion of benign hypertension.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a benign-hypertension change). Reduplication/thickening of elastic tissue (elastosis) occurs in the walls of muscular arteries in benign hypertension.
explanations.D: Correct. Necrosis — specifically fibrinoid necrosis of arteriolar walls — is a feature of MALIGNANT, not benign, hypertension. Benign hypertension produces slow, non-necrotising wall changes (hyalinosis, fibrosis, elastosis, medial hypertrophy); frank necrosis of the wall marks the accelerated/malignant phase. Recognising that the wall changes of benign hypertension are adaptive-degenerative rather than necrotising is the point of this question.

questions.learning_objective: List the benign-hypertension arterial wall changes (hyalinosis, fibrosis, elastosis) and recognise fibrinoid necrosis as a malignant, not benign, feature.

questions.title: Kidney surface in benign hypertension
questions.question: The surface of the kidney in benign hypertension is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A perfectly smooth surface is the normal kidney; benign hypertensive nephrosclerosis makes the surface finely granular, not smooth.
explanations.B: Correct. Benign nephrosclerosis (the renal lesion of benign hypertension) produces symmetrically contracted kidneys with a FINELY GRANULAR (‘leather-grain’) surface. The fine granularity results from hyaline arteriolosclerosis narrowing arterioles, causing diffuse patchy ischaemic atrophy and scarring of nephrons over a fine scale. This contrasts with the coarse, irregular scars of chronic pyelonephritis and with the petechial ‘flea-bitten’ kidney of the malignant phase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A coarsely irregular, deeply scarred surface points to chronic pyelonephritis or infarct scars, not the fine, even granularity of benign nephrosclerosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A ‘flea-bitten’ kidney (fine petechial haemorrhages on the surface) is the appearance of MALIGNANT hypertension, not benign.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the finely granular surface of the kidney in benign nephrosclerosis, distinguishing it from the flea-bitten malignant kidney.

questions.title: True statement about benign hypertension
questions.question: In benign hypertension, which of the followings is true:

options.A: It's less common than malignant hypertension
options.D: Atheroma formation is less severe than malignant hypertension

explanations.A: Incorrect. Benign hypertension is far MORE common than malignant hypertension; the great majority of hypertensives have the benign (chronic) form.
explanations.B: Correct. Benign hypertension causes symmetrical benign nephrosclerosis, so BOTH kidneys are diffusely and symmetrically contracted (small, finely granular). The lesion is bilateral because the raised systemic pressure and hyaline arteriolosclerosis affect both kidneys equally. This bilateral symmetrical contraction is a key gross feature distinguishing hypertensive nephrosclerosis from unilateral scarring processes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles is a feature of MALIGNANT hypertension; benign hypertension shows hyaline arteriolosclerosis instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Atheroma (atherosclerosis) is accelerated by hypertension; there is no rule that atheroma is milder in benign than malignant hypertension — this is not a true distinguishing statement.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that benign hypertension is common and causes bilateral symmetrical renal contraction, not fibrinoid necrosis.

questions.title: Change not shown by arterioles in malignant hypertension
questions.question: In malignant hypertension, arterioles don't show:

explanations.A: Incorrect (arterioles DO show this in malignant hypertension). Fibrinoid necrosis of the arteriolar wall is the defining acute lesion of malignant hypertension.
explanations.B: Incorrect (arterioles DO show this). Endothelial swelling/proliferation (endotheliosis) accompanies the acute arteriolar injury of the malignant phase.
explanations.C: Correct. Elastosis (reduplication of elastic tissue) is a slow, chronic adaptive change of BENIGN hypertension, not a feature of the acute arteriolar injury of malignant hypertension. Malignant hypertension is characterised instead by fibrinoid necrosis, endothelial injury, and hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis with concentric wall thickening. The distinction being tested is chronic elastic-tissue change (benign) versus acute necrotising and proliferative arteriolar injury (malignant).
explanations.D: Incorrect (arterioles DO show this). Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis produces concentric, laminated (onion-skin) THICKENING of the arteriolar wall in malignant hypertension.

questions.learning_objective: List the arteriolar changes of malignant hypertension (fibrinoid necrosis, endotheliosis, hyperplastic wall thickening) and exclude elastosis, a benign-phase change.

questions.title: Commonest cause of death in benign hypertension
questions.question: The most common cause of death in benign hypertension is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cerebral haemorrhage is an important hypertensive complication but is not the commonest cause of death in the benign form.
explanations.B: Correct. In benign hypertension the chronically raised afterload drives progressive left ventricular hypertrophy and eventual congestive HEART FAILURE, which is the commonest cause of death. The heart is the organ that bears the sustained pressure load longest, so ischaemic heart disease and hypertensive heart failure dominate mortality in chronic benign hypertension. This contrasts with malignant hypertension, where acute renal failure is the leading cause of death.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acute renal failure is the leading cause of death in MALIGNANT hypertension, not benign.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Although benign nephrosclerosis can cause slow renal impairment, chronic renal failure is not the commonest cause of death; heart failure is.

questions.learning_objective: State that heart failure is the commonest cause of death in benign hypertension.

questions.title: Commonest cause of death in malignant hypertension
questions.question: The most common cause of death in malignant hypertension is:

explanations.A: Correct. Malignant hypertension causes acute fibrinoid necrosis of renal arterioles and glomerular capillaries (malignant nephrosclerosis), producing rapidly progressive ACUTE RENAL FAILURE, which is the commonest cause of death. The kidney bears the brunt of the acute necrotising small-vessel injury of the malignant phase, so uraemia dominates the outcome. This is the classic contrast with benign hypertension, where death is usually from heart failure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Congestive heart failure is the commonest cause of death in BENIGN hypertension, not the malignant form.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cerebral haemorrhage and hypertensive encephalopathy do occur in malignant hypertension but are not the single commonest cause of death.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Respiratory failure is not a characteristic mode of death in malignant hypertension.

questions.learning_objective: State that acute renal failure is the commonest cause of death in malignant hypertension.

questions.title: True statement about malignant hypertension
questions.question: In malignant hypertension:

options.A: It's more common than benign hypertension

explanations.A: Incorrect. Malignant hypertension is much LESS common than benign hypertension; it is the accelerated form affecting a small minority.
explanations.B: Incorrect. In malignant hypertension the kidneys are typically normal-sized or slightly enlarged with a petechial ‘flea-bitten’ surface, not the small contracted kidneys of chronic benign nephrosclerosis.
explanations.C: Correct. The defining arteriolar lesion of malignant hypertension is FIBRINOID NECROSIS of the wall (with hyperplastic ‘onion-skin’ arteriolosclerosis), reflecting acute severe endothelial injury from the very high pressure. This necrotising small-vessel injury is what drives the rapid organ damage — malignant nephrosclerosis, retinopathy and encephalopathy — of the malignant phase. It is the single most characteristic microscopic feature distinguishing malignant from benign hypertension.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Papilloedema is CHARACTERISTIC of malignant hypertension (grade IV hypertensive retinopathy), not rare.

questions.learning_objective: Identify fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles as the defining lesion of malignant hypertension, which is less common than the benign form and features papilloedema.

questions.title: Lesion not part of hypertension
questions.question: The pathological lesions of hypertension include all of the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a hypertensive lesion). Elastosis (elastic-tissue reduplication) of arterioles/small arteries is part of the wall change of benign hypertension.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a hypertensive lesion). Necrotising arteriolitis (fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles) is the hallmark lesion of malignant hypertension.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a hypertensive lesion). Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis — concentric cellular (smooth-muscle) hyperplasia forming the onion-skin lesion — occurs in malignant hypertension.
explanations.D: Correct. A MYCOTIC aneurysm is caused by infection of the arterial wall (classically from septic emboli in infective endocarditis), weakening it — it is an infective, not a hypertensive, lesion. Hypertension is instead associated with Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms of small penetrating cerebral arteries and with accelerated atherosclerotic (e.g. berry-aneurysm rupture) risk, but the wall infection of a mycotic aneurysm has a different mechanism entirely, which is why it is the exception.

questions.learning_objective: List the vascular lesions of hypertension (elastosis, necrotising arteriolitis, hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis) and recognise a mycotic aneurysm as an infective, not hypertensive, lesion.

questions.title: Vascular lesion in long-standing moderate hypertension
questions.question: A 45 year old male patient with blood pressure ranging from 150/90 to 160/95 mm Hg for the past 10 years. Which of the following vascular lesions is most likely to be found in this patient:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis is the lesion of MALIGNANT/accelerated hypertension with markedly elevated pressures, not the moderate, long-standing (benign) hypertension described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Granulomatous arteritis (e.g. giant-cell or Takayasu arteritis) is an inflammatory large/medium-artery disease, unrelated to chronic benign hypertension.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-inflammatory renal-artery wall disease that can CAUSE renovascular hypertension in young women; it is not the arteriolar lesion PRODUCED by chronic moderate hypertension.
explanations.D: Correct. Ten years of moderate (benign) hypertension produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis — homogeneous glassy pink thickening of arteriolar walls from plasma-protein leakage and increased matrix. This is the characteristic small-vessel lesion of long-standing benign hypertension (and diabetes), narrowing the lumen slowly. The moderate pressure and long duration point to the bland hyaline lesion rather than the necrotising/hyperplastic lesions of the malignant form.

questions.learning_objective: Match long-standing moderate (benign) hypertension to hyaline arteriolosclerosis.

questions.title: Renal biopsy in severe accelerated hypertension
questions.question: A young man suffered from severe headache and blurring of vision. His blood pressure is 250/160 mm Hg. Urine analysis shows proteinuria. Renal biopsy will show:

options.B: Hyalinization of the walls of arterioles
options.C: Fibrinoid necrosis of the walls of arterioles

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glomerular hyalinisation is a chronic sclerotic end-change, not the acute lesion of a hypertensive emergency at 250/160 mm Hg.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hyaline change of arteriolar walls is the lesion of BENIGN (chronic moderate) hypertension; the extreme pressure and acute presentation here point to the malignant lesion instead.
explanations.C: Correct. The picture — a young man, severe headache and visual blurring (papilloedema), 250/160 mm Hg and proteinuria — is malignant (accelerated) hypertension, whose renal lesion is FIBRINOID NECROSIS of arteriolar walls (malignant nephrosclerosis), often with a hyperplastic onion-skin change. The acute severe endothelial injury from the very high pressure lets fibrin and plasma proteins deposit in the necrotic wall. This necrotising arteriolar lesion is precisely what distinguishes the malignant phase from the bland hyaline change of benign hypertension.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Renal infarction is a localised ischaemic event (e.g. from embolism); it is not the diffuse arteriolar lesion of malignant hypertension shown on biopsy.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise malignant hypertension clinically and name fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles as its renal biopsy lesion.

questions.title: Complication not caused by decompensated benign hypertension
questions.question: Decompensated benign hypertension can cause all of the followings except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a complication). Benign hypertension raises left ventricular afterload, causing left ventricular hypertrophy and, on decompensation, LEFT-sided heart failure.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a complication). Chronic benign nephrosclerosis can progress to renal impairment/failure.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a complication). Left-sided failure raises pulmonary venous pressure and pulmonary arterial resistance, leading in turn to RIGHT-sided failure (backward failure), so right-sided HF can follow.
explanations.D: Correct. Retinopathy severe enough to cause blindness (with papilloedema, flame haemorrhages and exudates) is a feature of MALIGNANT (accelerated) hypertension, not decompensated benign hypertension. Benign hypertension produces only mild grade I–II retinal changes (arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking). Sight-threatening grade IV retinopathy belongs to the malignant phase, which is the distinction this question draws.

questions.learning_objective: List complications of decompensated benign hypertension (left then right heart failure, renal failure) and recognise blinding retinopathy as a malignant-phase feature.

questions.title: Etiology of essential hypertension
questions.question: Which of the following is an etiology of essential hypertension:

explanations.A: Correct. Essential (primary) hypertension has no single identifiable cause but arises from interacting factors, of which IMPAIRED RENAL SODIUM EXCRETION is central: a kidney that cannot excrete a sodium load at normal pressure retains sodium and water, expands plasma volume and resets pressure upward. This defect, together with genetic predisposition and altered vasoconstrictor/vasodilator balance, defines the multifactorial mechanism of essential hypertension. The other options are all identifiable causes of SECONDARY, not essential, hypertension.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Renal artery stenosis is a renovascular cause of SECONDARY hypertension (identifiable cause), not essential.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phaeochromocytoma is an adrenal-medullary catecholamine-secreting tumour causing SECONDARY hypertension.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Coarctation of the aorta is a mechanical/cardiovascular cause of SECONDARY hypertension.

questions.learning_objective: Identify impaired renal sodium excretion as a mechanism of essential hypertension, distinguishing it from identifiable secondary causes.

questions.title: Afferent arteriole in polycystic-kidney hypertension
questions.question: A 50 years old male patient complaining of polycystic kidney, for which his physician recommended nephrectomy and renal transplantation. The AFFERENT arterioles of his excised kidney will show:

options.B: Two layers of the internal elastic lamina and thick media
options.C: Glassy pink thickening of the intima and media
options.D: Concentric alternating layers of smooth muscles and connective tissue

explanations.A: Incorrect. Granular eosinophilic ‘fibrin-like’ material describes FIBRINOID necrosis, the lesion of malignant hypertension, not the chronic hyaline change expected here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reduplication of the internal elastic lamina with a thick media describes a muscular-artery/elastosis change, not the arteriolar lesion being asked about.
explanations.C: Correct. Chronic hypertension (here secondary to polycystic kidney disease) produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis: the afferent arterioles show homogeneous GLASSY PINK (hyaline) thickening of the wall (intima and media) from plasma-protein insudation and matrix accumulation, narrowing the lumen. This is the classic bland small-vessel lesion of long-standing benign-type hypertension. ‘Glassy pink thickening’ is simply the histological description of hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Concentric alternating (onion-skin) layers describe HYPERPLASTIC arteriolosclerosis of malignant hypertension, not the chronic hyaline change here.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise ‘glassy pink thickening’ of afferent arterioles as hyaline arteriolosclerosis in chronic hypertension.

questions.title: Pathological changes in malignant hypertension
questions.question: Pathological changes in malignant hypertension include:

options.B: Concentric hypertrophy of the left ventricle

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer. Hyaline arteriosclerosis (a chronic hypertensive change) can coexist on a background of pre-existing hypertension, so it is included — but it is not the only correct option.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer. Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy from pressure overload is present, but it is not the only correct option.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer. Hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis is characteristic of the malignant phase, but it is not the only correct option.
explanations.D: Correct. Malignant hypertension usually arises on a background of pre-existing hypertension, so the kidney and vessels can show ALL of these: pre-existing hyaline arteriosclerosis, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic pressure overload, and the superimposed acute hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis of the accelerated phase. Because each listed change genuinely occurs, ‘all of the above’ is the correct answer. The key idea is that malignant hypertension is superimposed acceleration, layering acute lesions on chronic hypertensive changes.

questions.learning_objective: State that malignant hypertension can show hyaline arteriosclerosis, concentric LVH and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis together.

questions.title: Not a major risk factor of atherosclerosis
questions.question: Which of the following is not a major risk factor of atherosclerosis:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a major risk factor). Hypertension is one of the major modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis, injuring endothelium and accelerating plaque formation.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a major risk factor). Diabetes mellitus is a major risk factor, roughly doubling atherosclerotic risk through dyslipidaemia and endothelial injury.
explanations.C: Correct. A HIGH level of HDL (‘good’ cholesterol) is PROTECTIVE against atherosclerosis, not a risk factor — HDL carries cholesterol away from vessel walls back to the liver (reverse cholesterol transport). It is a LOW HDL that raises risk. Listing high HDL among risk factors reverses its actual protective role, which is exactly what this question tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS a major risk factor). A high level of LDL (‘bad’ cholesterol) is a central major risk factor, depositing cholesterol in the intima to form plaques.

questions.learning_objective: List the major risk factors of atherosclerosis (hypertension, diabetes, high LDL) and recognise high HDL as protective, not a risk factor.

questions.title: The 'good' cholesterol
questions.question: The term "good" cholesterol is used to describe:

explanations.A: Incorrect. VLDL carries endogenous triglyceride from the liver and is a precursor of LDL; it is not the ‘good’ cholesterol.
explanations.B: Incorrect. LDL is the ‘bad’ cholesterol — it delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissues and, in excess, into the arterial intima to form atheroma.
explanations.C: Correct. HIGH-density lipoprotein (HDL) is termed the ‘good’ cholesterol because it performs reverse cholesterol transport, carrying cholesterol from peripheral tissues and vessel walls back to the liver for excretion. A high HDL level is therefore protective against atherosclerosis, which is why it is nicknamed ‘good’. This is the mirror image of LDL, the ‘bad’ cholesterol that deposits lipid in the intima.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ‘Pre-beta lipoprotein’ is the electrophoretic band corresponding to VLDL, not HDL (which runs in the alpha band).

questions.learning_objective: Identify HDL as the ‘good’ (protective) cholesterol that performs reverse cholesterol transport.

questions.title: Vessels affected by atherosclerosis
questions.question: Atherosclerosis affects:

explanations.A: Correct. Atherosclerosis is a disease of ARTERIES — specifically the intima of large elastic arteries (aorta, carotid, iliac) and medium muscular arteries (coronary, popliteal) — where lipid-laden atheromatous plaques form. It does not affect veins or the myocardium directly; its damage to the heart is indirect, through coronary-artery narrowing causing ischaemia. Naming the artery as the target vessel is the basic definition being tested.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Veins are not affected by atherosclerosis (they may undergo other changes such as phlebosclerosis or varicosity, but not atheroma).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The myocardium is injured only SECONDARILY (ischaemia/infarction) when coronary arteries are diseased; atherosclerosis is not a primary myocardial disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Because veins and myocardium are not primary targets, ‘all of the above’ is wrong; atherosclerosis is an arterial disease.

questions.learning_objective: State that atherosclerosis is a disease of the arterial intima, not of veins or myocardium.

questions.title: Nature of atherosclerosis (per source)
questions.question: Atherosclerosis is a/an:

explanations.A: Incorrect per this source. Modern pathology does increasingly describe atherosclerosis as having a chronic inflammatory component (the response-to-injury hypothesis), but the answer keyed in this department-style bank is ‘degenerative disease’ — so ‘inflammatory’ is not the intended answer here.
explanations.B: Correct (per this source). This bank classifies atherosclerosis as a DEGENERATIVE arterial disease — a chronic, age-related degeneration of the intima with lipid deposition, fibrosis and calcification of the vessel wall. The term captures the slow, wear-and-deposition nature of plaque build-up in large and medium arteries. (Note for the learner: contemporary teaching also emphasises a chronic inflammatory/response-to-injury element, but the classification asked for here is degenerative.)
explanations.C: Incorrect. Atherosclerosis is not an autoimmune disease; there is no autoantibody-mediated attack on the artery driving it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Atherosclerosis is not an embolic lesion — emboli (e.g. cholesterol emboli) are a COMPLICATION of established plaques, not the nature of the disease itself.

questions.author_notes: Source keys this B (degenerative). Modern consensus stresses a chronic inflammatory/response-to-injury component; explanation flags this while authoring to the printed key, per exam-faithfulness protocol.
questions.learning_objective: State the source's classification of atherosclerosis as a degenerative arterial disease (noting the modern inflammatory view).

questions.title: Most important risk factor under 45 years
questions.question: The most important risk factor for atherosclerosis in patients under 45 years is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Smoking is an important modifiable risk factor for atherosclerosis, but in the under-45 group hyperlipidaemia is singled out as the most important.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Male sex is a non-modifiable risk factor, but it is not the single most important factor in the young.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Physical inactivity contributes to risk but is a lesser, indirect factor compared with hyperlipidaemia in young patients.
explanations.D: Correct. In patients under 45 years, HYPERLIPIDAEMIA (especially familial/genetic dyslipidaemias with very high LDL) is the most important risk factor for premature atherosclerosis, because a lifelong high LDL burden drives early, aggressive intimal lipid deposition. Severe inherited hypercholesterolaemia can cause clinically significant atherosclerosis and coronary disease at an unusually young age. This is why a young patient with premature atherosclerosis is investigated for a lipid disorder first.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hyperlipidaemia as the most important atherosclerosis risk factor in patients under 45.

questions.title: Not a major atherosclerosis risk factor
questions.question: Major risk factors for the development of atherosclerosis include all of the following lesions except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a major risk factor). Cigarette smoking is a major modifiable risk factor, promoting endothelial injury and atherogenesis.
explanations.B: Correct. HYPOcholesterolaemia (a LOW blood cholesterol) is not a risk factor for atherosclerosis — it is HYPERcholesterolaemia (high cholesterol, especially high LDL) that drives plaque formation. Naming a low cholesterol as a risk factor reverses the actual lipid relationship, so it is the exception. The genuine major risk factors are hypertension, diabetes mellitus, smoking and hyperlipidaemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a major risk factor). Hypertension is a major modifiable risk factor for atherosclerosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS a major risk factor). Diabetes mellitus is a major risk factor, accelerating atherosclerosis through dyslipidaemia and endothelial damage.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise hypocholesterolaemia as not a risk factor for atherosclerosis (hypercholesterolaemia is).
